subject: Clarification: Egress controls, bastionless access, and threat mitigations
messages:
From: Mike Rodriguez <mike.rodriguez@acmecorp.com>
To: irene.choi@redwood.ai, security@acmecorp.com
Date: Thu, 20 May 2027 15:12:00 -0700
Subject: Questions on egress policy and bastionless deployment

Hi Irene,

Thanks for the quick turnaround on the RFI. We had a few follow-ups from our infra/security team about your 'bastionless' private deployment option and how egress is controlled:

1) How does Redwood ensure there is no uncontrolled outbound TCP/UDP egress from inference nodes?
2) Can you describe the telemetry available for egress events (per-tenant, per-IP, per-process)?
3) We need an attacker model explaining residual risk if a sidecar proxy is compromised.

If possible, could you share a network diagram and a short threat-playbook that maps the likely attack vectors to mitigations and controls? We will circulate to procurement and SOC.

Appreciate it — Mike

--
Mike Rodriguez
Director, Infrastructure Security
AcmeCorp
From: Irene Choi <irene.choi@redwood.ai>
To: Mike Rodriguez <mike.rodriguez@acmecorp.com>, Alice Wong <alice.wong@acmecorp.com>
Cc: vanessa.ortiz@redwood.ai, karthik.iyer@redwood.ai
Date: Fri, 21 May 2027 09:08:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Questions on egress policy and bastionless deployment

Hi Mike / Alice,

Thanks — great questions. Summary up front: Redwood Private supports a bastionless deployment model via enforced egress policies, host-level network fences, and an audited, token-scoped egress proxy. We attach a diagram and a short threat-playbook that maps attack vectors to mitigations. Key points:

- Outbound controls: We deploy per-cluster iptables/ebpf rules at the hypervisor/host level + cloud security groups (if in VPC) to restrict allowed egress to: our token-scoped egress proxy endpoints, customer-approved artifact registries, and customer-managed internal services. All other outbound destinations are denied by default.

- Egress proxy + token scoping: Each inference request that may call external artifacts (e.g., model weights, remote enrichment services) must obtain a short-lived, tenant-scoped egress token issued by the customer-facing control plane. Tokens are single-use for specific host/process categories and encoded with permitted FQDNs/IP ranges and time window. The proxy validates tokens and enforces destination allowlists.

- Telemetry / observability: We emit per-request egress records that include timestamp, tenant_id, pod/container id, process (sidecar or runtime), destination IP/FQDN, bytes transferred, and TLS SNI where available. Records are pushed to the customer’s audit stream (syslog/CloudWatch/GCS) and are also available in the Redwood Console under a tenant-scoped Events feed.

- Sidecar compromise model: If a sidecar is compromised, the most likely attack primitives are: outbound data exfiltration to allowed destinations and forging of internal API calls within the node boundary. Mitigations: token scoping (prevents arbitrary destinations), process-level mTLS to internal services, syscall filtering in the runtime sandbox, and prefix/KV cache integrity checks with HMACed keys.

Attached: egress-policy-diagram.png (network layout), rfi-threat-summary.pdf (threat mappings + mitigations), egress-logging-example.yaml (example event schema).

Next steps: 1) If you want, we can run a short 45m walkthrough with your infra and SOC to go through the diagram and logs schema. 2) We can provide a tailored egress allowlist template for your environment.

Let us know which time slot you prefer — we have availability Monday or Wednesday afternoon (PDT).

Best,
Irene

Subject: Re: Questions on egress policy and bastionless deployment

Irene,

Quick follow-up from SOC after reviewing the attachments — thanks for those. A couple of clarifying asks before we book the walkthrough:

- Can Redwood retain egress DNS/SNI records for 90 days in a tamper-evident way? We need to show historical lookbacks during incident response.
- For deployments inside our VPC, can we enforce that the egress proxy sits in a customer-managed subnet (not a Redwood-managed subnet)?
- Are there hard limits or recovery procedures if the token-issuance service becomes unavailable?

Also — can you confirm which of the attachments is the canonical diagram we should reference in procurement?

Thanks,
Alice

Alice Wong
Security Engineer, AcmeCorp
From: Irene Choi <irene.choi@redwood.ai>
To: Alice Wong <alice.wong@acmecorp.com>, Mike Rodriguez <mike.rodriguez@acmecorp.com>
Cc: vanessa.ortiz@redwood.ai, karthik.iyer@redwood.ai
Date: Sat, 22 May 2027 09:45:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Questions on egress policy and bastionless deployment

Hi Alice / Mike,

Thanks — answers below and brief operational notes.

- Retention: Yes. We support sending raw egress events to your customer-controlled log sink (S3/GCS/CloudWatch). For tamper-evidence, we provide an optional append-only audit stream backed by an HSM-signed checkpointing service; we can retain DNS/SNI metadata for 90+ days. We will include a short appendix in the walkthrough showing the signed checkpoint verification steps.

- Customer-managed egress proxy: Yes. For Private deployments inside a VPC, the egress proxy (reverse-validated token gateway) can be deployed in a customer-managed subnet behind your NAT/Gateway. Redwood will provide deployment manifests and a hardened proxy image; the proxy authenticates with the Redwood control plane but connects over your private peering. This model is what we recommend for regulated deployments.

- Token service availability: Tokens are short-lived but we provide an active-active token-issuance pair with local caching in the control plane. If the issuance service becomes unavailable, hosts operate in a conservative fail-closed mode by default (blocked outbound) but can be configured with a short grace window (configurable) that permits previously cached, still-valid tokens to be accepted. Any relaxed mode is tracked in the audit stream and flagged in Console alerts.

- Canonical diagram: egress-policy-diagram.png is the canonical network diagram (v3). Link: https://drive.redwood.ai/shared/ACME/egress-diagram-v3. Procurement should reference the diagram plus the rfi-threat-summary.pdf for mitigations mapping.

Operational notes for the walkthrough: please share a preferred 45m slot and we will include an engineer from our runtime security team (Karthik) and a product PM (Vanessa) to review SLA/retention options.

Next steps: I will put an availability poll in a follow-up; if procurement wants an allowlist template first I can attach one.

Best regards,
Irene
